notes.meaning: The south gate of the outer court was built just like the east and north gates. It had the same windows and the same size: fifty cubits long and twenty-five wide. A cubit is a measure of about the length of a forearm. Matthew Henry sees the many windows as a picture of the light God gives his church through his word.

Seven steps led up into this gate, with palm trees carved on the pillars, as at the other gates. Matthew Henry says the steps remind us to keep growing in grace, step by step, toward heaven. The palm trees picture God's people flourishing in his house and winning over their spiritual enemies (Psalm 92:12).

Straight across from the outer south gate stood a south gate into the inner court. The space between the two gates was a hundred cubits, the same as on the east and north. There was no gate on the west side of either court.

The guide walked Ezekiel from the outer south gate, across the pavement, and in through the inner south gate. He measured it, and it matched the outer gates in every part. Matthew Henry draws a lesson from this. God's grace works the same way in mature Christians as in beginners. The mature have simply come nearer to being complete.

This short note gives one more measurement for the inner gates. Adam Clarke thinks a word has dropped out, and that the five cubits should read twenty-five, to match the other verses. He also notes that some old copies leave the whole verse out. Keil & Delitzsch accept the verse and think it gives the thickness of the gate's side walls.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Several scholars think this verse was added to the text later, because the old Greek translation leaves it out and its numbers are hard to fit.

notes.meaning: The inner gates were built facing the other way. Their porches pointed out toward the outer court. The outer gates had seven steps, but the inner gates had eight. Matthew Henry says this teaches that the nearer we come to God, the higher we should rise above this world.

Next the guide measured the east gate of the inner court. This court was the priests' court, next to the temple itself. Like the south gate, it had the same rooms, pillars, windows and size as the others. It too had palm carvings and eight steps.

Last came the north gate of the inner court. It matched the others too, with its windows, palm trees and eight steps. Matthew Henry says the careful, repeated detail shows how closely God notices everything and everyone that belongs to his church.

Next to the gate stood a small room with a door. There the burnt offering was washed. (A burnt offering was an animal burned whole on the altar.) Some say this room was only at the north gate, since the law had sacrifices killed north of the altar. Others say there was one at each inner gate. Matthew Henry says that before we come near God, we must wash our hands and our hearts.

In the gate's porch stood tables for the sacrifices. These were the burnt offering, the sin offering (to deal with sin) and the guilt offering (to make up for wrongs). Keil & Delitzsch say the tables held the meat, and the killing was done just outside. Matthew Henry reads the passage as a picture of the many spiritual sacrifices offered to God in the gospel age.

differ.view: This describes a real temple during Christ's future thousand-year reign. Its sacrifices will look back to the cross as a reminder, much as the Lord's Supper does now.

notes.meaning: There were eight tables in all: four inside the porch and four outside it, two on each side. Matthew Henry notes that neither the tabernacle nor Solomon's temple had tables like these. He takes them as a sign of the great number of people who would bring spiritual offerings to God in gospel times.

Four more tables were made of cut stone. Each was about a cubit and a half square and a cubit high. On them lay the knives and tools used for the sacrifices. Keil & Delitzsch think these tables stood by the steps.

Hooks about a hand's width long were fixed to the walls. The meat could hang on them while it was made ready, and the flesh of the offering was laid on the tables. Matthew Henry says everything was set out so the offering would be ready for the altar.

Inside the inner court were two rooms, one by the north gate and one by the south gate, facing each other. Older translations call them rooms for the singers. Matthew Henry takes that reading to mean that Christians should be singers, full of praise. Keil & Delitzsch point out that the next verses make these rooms for priests.

The guide explained that the room facing south was for the priests who looked after the temple. They took turns caring for it and its service, keeping it clean and kept in repair, and guarding it from anything unholy. Matthew Henry says God provides a place for all who serve in his house.

The room facing north was for the priests in charge of the altar, who kept its fire burning. These were the sons of Zadok. Zadok came from Aaron's family and stayed loyal when others rebelled against King Solomon. So only his family could come near the Lord to serve at the altar.

The priests' court was a perfect square, a hundred cubits each way, and the altar stood in front of the temple. Matthew Henry notes that with the gates open, people in the outer court could see the altar. He says Christ is our altar and our sacrifice, the one we look to whenever we come to God.

Now the guide led Ezekiel to the porch of the temple building itself. Several commentators say this really begins the next chapter. The doorway seems to have had two folding doors. Matthew Henry says the porch teaches us not to rush into God's presence, but to come slowly and with reverence.

The porch was twenty cubits by twelve, with steps leading up to it. The Hebrew text says eleven cubits; twelve and the ten steps come from the old Greek translation. Two columns stood by the pillars, like the columns Jachin and Boaz at Solomon's temple. Matthew Henry says that in the church, everything should be firm and done decently and in order.
